messages.content: How do I find the angle of the force for a given momentum?

function.name: calculate_vector_angle
function.description: Calculate the angle of a vector based on its X and Y components. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

X_component.description: The X component of the vector. This is a float type value.

Y_component.description: The Y component of the vector. This is a float type value.

use_degrees.description: If true, the result will be in degrees. If false, the result will be in radians. Default is false.

message.reasoning:
The user asks: "How do I find the angle of the force for a given momentum?" They want to know how to find the angle of the force for a given momentum. We need to respond with an explanation. Possibly they want to use the relationship between force and momentum: F = dp/dt. But if we have momentum vector p(t) at two times, we can compute average force as Δp/Δt. Then the direction of force is same as change in momentum. So angle of force relative to some axis can be found from components of Δp. Use arctan2(Δpy, Δpx). Or if we have instantaneous momentum p(t), then differentiate to get velocity v = p/m. Force direction is acceleration direction. But maybe they want to find angle of force vector given momentum magnitude and direction? Actually question: "How do I find the angle of the force for a given momentum?" Might be ambiguous. Provide general method: For a particle of mass m, momentum p = m v. Force is derivative of momentum: F = dp/dt. So if you know momentum as function of time, differentiate to get force vector. Then angle of force relative to coordinate axes: θ = atan2(F_y, F_x). If only magnitude of momentum known but not direction, cannot determine force direction without additional info.

We should ask clarifying question: Do you have momentum components or just magnitude? Also what coordinate system? Provide formula: θ_F = atan2(dp_y/dt, dp_x/dt). If momentum changes linearly over small interval Δt, approximate F ≈ Δp / Δt. Then angle = atan2(Δp_y, Δp_x).

Also mention that if momentum is constant, force zero. So no angle. Provide example: Suppose momentum changes from (p1x,p1y) to (p2x,p2y) over Δt. Compute Δp = (p2x-p1x, p2y-p1y). Then F_avg = Δp/Δt. Angle = atan2(Δp_y, Δp_x). Provide code snippet using python's math.atan2. Also note that if you want degrees, convert rad to deg.

Thus answer: explain concept, provide formula, ask clarifying question.
